options.text: Thicker in the middle than at the edges
Thinner in the middle than at the edges

questions.explanation: A converging (convex) lens is thicker in the middle than at the edges. It brings parallel light rays together to a focus.

questions.stem: The principal focus of a converging lens is the point where:

options.text: Parallel rays of light converge after passing through the lens

questions.explanation: The principal focus (F) is the point where parallel rays of light converge after passing through a converging lens.

questions.stem: The focal length of a lens is:

options.text: The distance from the object to the lens
The distance from the lens to the image
The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus

questions.explanation: The focal length is the distance from the optical centre of the lens to the principal focus. A shorter focal length means a more powerful lens.
A diverging lens always produces a virtual, upright, diminished image, regardless of where the object is placed.

questions.stem: When using a converging lens as a magnifying glass, the object must be placed:

options.text: Between the lens and the principal focus

questions.explanation: To use a converging lens as a magnifying glass, the object is placed between the lens and the principal focus. This produces a virtual, upright, magnified image.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a real image and a virtual image?

options.text: Real images are larger; virtual images are smaller
Real images can be projected onto a screen; virtual images cannot
Virtual images are brighter than real images

questions.explanation: A real image is formed where light rays actually converge and can be projected onto a screen. A virtual image appears where light rays seem to come from but do not actually meet.
Short-sightedness means distant objects are focused in front of the retina. A diverging lens spreads the light slightly before it enters the eye, moving the focus point back onto the retina.
